Each location has one standard name in this package, such as `Kenya`, `United_States` or `Cote_dIvoire`, but people write country names in many other ways. This page covers which names are recognized and what happens when one isn't.

```{python}
import starsim_data as ssd

[ssd.resolve(name) for name in ['Kenya', 'kenya', 'KE', 'KEN', 'Republic of Kenya']]
```

## What is recognized

These forms are all recognized:

| Form | Example | Resolves to |
|---|---|---|
| Standard name | `United_States` | `United_States` |
| Free-text name | `united states` | `United_States` |
| ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 | `US` | `United_States` |
| ISO 3166-1 alpha-3 | `USA` | `United_States` |
| Official name | `United States of America` | `United_States` |
| Common abbreviation | `DRC`, `UK`, `UAE` | the corresponding country |
| Former name | `Zaire`, `Burma` | the current country |
| French, Spanish or Portuguese name | `Allemagne`, `Alemania` | `Germany` |

Accents, case, punctuation and spacing are ignored, so these are all treated as the same name:

```{python}
{name: ssd.locations.normalize(name) for name in
 ["Côte d'Ivoire", "cote divoire", "Cote_dIvoire", "  COTE D'IVOIRE  "]}
```

```{python}
len(set(ssd.resolve(n) for n in ["Côte d'Ivoire", 'cote divoire', 'Ivory Coast', 'CIV']))
```

## Resolution is exact; approximate matching only advises

A name has to match one in the table exactly (after ignoring accents, case and punctuation). Close matches are only used to suggest names in the error message; the package never guesses which country you meant.

```{python}
#| error: true
ssd.load('Keyna', which='deaths')
```

Guessing would go wrong both ways. Abbreviations like `USA` look nothing like `United_States`, so they have to be listed in the table rather than guessed. And a name that is no country at all still has close matches:

```{python}
import sciris as sc
sc.suggest('Atlantis', ssd.list_all_locations(), n=3, die=False)
```

That is helpful in an error message, but would be wrong as an answer.

## Subnational units

A subnational unit is named by its country and its own name, separated by a colon, as in the node table's `dot_name`. The country part is recognized as above; the unit's name has to match exactly, ignoring case, accents and punctuation:

```{python}
[ssd.resolve(name) for name in ['United States:Massachusetts', 'USA:massachusetts', 'us:new york']]
```

When no dataset is given, the units are those of the node table, and a misspelled unit gets suggestions from its own country. Only a few datasets have subnational units so far: `mistry2021_us` and `population_us`, for the US states (see [Datasets](datasets.qmd#us-states)).

## Scoping to a dataset

Coverage varies between datasets, so `load()` checks the name against the locations in the dataset you asked for. A country that exists but is missing from that dataset gives a different error from a name that isn't a country at all:

```{python}
#| error: true
ssd.load('Japan', which='prem2021')
```

```{python}
len(ssd.list_locations('prem2021')), len(ssd.list_locations('mistry2021'))
```

`list_locations(which)` gives the locations in one dataset, and `list_all_locations()` gives every location the package knows about.

```{python}
len(ssd.list_all_locations())
```

## Inspecting the table

```{python}
info = ssd.location_info('DRC')
{k: info[k] for k in ['location', 'iso_code', 'iso3', 'official_name']}
```

```{python}
ssd.location_info('Germany').aliases[:8]
```

The table itself is `starsim_data/data/locations.csv`, with official names and aliases taken from the `pycountry` package. Any alias that could mean two different locations is left out, so a name that matches always means just one.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Namibia's country code
Namibia's two-letter ISO code is `NA`, which `pandas.read_csv` reads as a missing value by default. This package handles it, but if you read country tables with pandas yourself, pass `keep_default_na=False` to avoid losing Namibia.

```{python}
ssd.resolve('NA'), ssd.location_info('Namibia').iso3
```
:::

## Administrative levels

`parse_level()` accepts the common ways of writing an administrative level and returns a number:

```{python}
[ssd.parse_level(x) for x in ['admin1', 'ADM2', '3', 4, 'level0']]
```

Level 0 is the country, level 1 its first subdivisions (provinces, states), and so on. The highest is 5, the finest level any of the boundary sources in [Data sources](datasources.qmd) publishes.

```{python}
#| error: true
ssd.parse_level('admin9')
```

`True` and `False` are rejected, rather than quietly read as levels 1 and 0:

```{python}
#| error: true
ssd.parse_level(True)
```

## Naming below the country level

Subnational units in the node table are named by their `dot_name`, the country and unit names joined by a colon, cleaned up the same way but keeping capitals:

```{python}
ssd.load_nodes('France', level=1).dot_name.head(4).tolist()
```

```{python}
[ssd.node_name(x) for x in ['New York', 'Île-de-France', 'KwaZulu-Natal']]
```

The part before the colon is always a name `load()` accepts, so you can split a `dot_name` and look up its country directly. To join to other data, though, use `pcode` rather than `dot_name`; see [Spatial data](spatial.qmd).
